First off I don't really know what infinity is.

If you want, instead of the concept of infinity, you can think "by going far enough, I can make the second integral (in your picture) equal any number as high as I like."

Second, I have never been comfortable calling integrals the exact area.

for 1/x^2 and whether it's exact, you can think "there are numbers I can't reach, no matter how far I take this integral." (eg 1.111111..... will never reach 1.2 no matter how many digits you add). So you can imagine a set comprised of all the numbers you can achieve by following the integral further to the right, and you know this set is bounded.

ie There is some number x such that any number <x can be achieved by following the integral far enough, and any number >x can't be achieved no matter how far you follow the integral.

If I'm phrasing this reasonably and you're following along, then your doubts about the exactness of the indefinite integral is basically a question of whether x is contained in the set we've constructed. This is actually a pretty deep question and I can't think how to convince you simply. You can look into the least upper bound property if you want.

Both functions have limit 0 when x approaches infinity. In calculus infinities are kind of "equal", which does not make calculus very good field of maths for examining infinities. Set theory has a concept of cardinality which makes it possible to compare infinite sets. For example set of natural numbers is a countably infinite set, but set of real numbers is uncountably infinite and greater than the first one.

For some weird reason, I can't open the image you attached, but, yes, an integral can be a finete number, even if the interval of integration is infinite. When that happens, it is the area, exactly. There can be even weirder situations, a well known example is a solid of revolution that has finite volume, but infinite superficial area.

By saying that you are not comfortable calling an integral an "exact area", I think you are perhaps not completely comfortable with the concept of limits. Unfortunetly limits is usually not well taught introductory math courses. It is a tricky concept. If you want I could try to explain in more detail. Could you care to expand why do you find it uncomfortable?
